B2.title: Why Handwriting Still Matters
B2.text: Many people argue that handwriting is a skill we can safely abandon now that nearly everyone owns a keyboard. I believe this view is mistaken, or at least premature. Studies suggest that students who take notes by hand tend to remember more, because they are forced to summarise rather than copy. Writing slowly also gives the mind time to organise ideas before they reach the page. Of course, typing is faster, and nobody would deny that it is more practical for long documents. Nevertheless, speed is not the only measure of value. For that reason, I think schools should continue to teach handwriting, even if it occupies a smaller place in the timetable than before.

B2.title: How a Heat Pump Works
B2.text: A heat pump warms a house by moving heat rather than creating it. Even on a cold day, the air outside contains some warmth, which a liquid inside the machine absorbs and turns into gas. This gas is then compressed, and compression makes it much hotter, just as a bicycle pump becomes warm when it is used. The hot gas passes through a coil inside the house, where it gives up its heat and turns back into liquid. The cycle then begins again, repeating itself for as long as the machine is switched on. Because it transfers heat instead of burning fuel, a heat pump can deliver several times more energy than it consumes. This efficiency explains why such machines are becoming popular in countries with cold winters.

B2.title: My Grandfather's Workshop

He died shortly before I finished school, and the workshop was sold soon afterwards. Even now, the smell of fresh sawdust brings back those long quiet afternoons so vividly that I have to stop for a moment.

C1.title: A Translator's Tuesday
C1.text: Marta works from home as a literary translator, a job that sounds more glamorous than it is. Her mornings are devoted to the hardest passages, since she has learned that her concentration fades long before lunch. She spends hours agonising over a single sentence, weighing whether a particular word captures the author's tone or merely approximates it. By early afternoon, she usually switches to emails and invoices, tasks that demand little imagination but must nevertheless be done. Her neighbours assume that she has endless free time, and they are forever knocking on her door to ask for small favours. She has stopped explaining that working at home is still working, because the explanation rarely seems to register. In the evening she takes a long walk, which she regards as part of the job rather than a break from it. Ideas that had refused to come at her desk have a way of arriving unannounced between the river and the market. When she finally returns, she reads her morning's work aloud, listening for any false notes that her eyes might have missed.

C1.title: Across the Desert by Road
C1.text: We set out before dawn, hoping to cross the worst of the desert before the heat became unbearable. The road looked straight and simple on the map, but it was pitted with holes that forced us to crawl at a pace that would have embarrassed a cyclist. By midday the thermometer on the dashboard had climbed past forty degrees, and the air inside the car felt thick enough to chew. Our guide, a taciturn man named Idris, seemed untroubled and spent most of the journey humming to himself. When the engine finally gave up, he lifted the bonnet, studied it for a long moment, and announced that the problem was nothing but a loose cable. Within ten minutes we were moving again, though I suspect that his calm owed more to experience than to any great mechanical talent. That evening we reached a small oasis where the villagers, who had not expected visitors, insisted on feeding us dates and sweet tea. Looking back, I remember the discomfort only dimly, whereas the generosity of those strangers remains as sharp as ever. It is a lesson in how little people need in order to be kind.

qs.q: Why did the travellers leave before dawn?
o: To avoid the worst of the heat

qs.q: What was wrong with the engine?
o: It had run out of fuel

qs.q: What does the writer suspect about Idris's calm?
o: It was an act to impress the travellers
It came from experience rather than great talent
It came from not caring about the journey
It came from knowing the oasis was close

qs.q: What does the writer remember most clearly?

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what happened to the travellers, and what did they remember most?

C1.title: A Polite Refusal
C1.text: Dear Helena, thank you for your generous invitation to join the committee, which I read with both pride and a degree of guilt. After careful thought, I have concluded that I must decline, not for lack of enthusiasm but because I am already stretched thinner than is sensible. Over the past year I have accepted several commitments that seemed manageable on their own, only to find that together they leave no room to breathe. I would rather do a few things properly than appear on every list and contribute little. That said, I would be delighted to help in a more limited capacity, perhaps by reviewing documents or speaking at your annual meeting. Should either of these prove useful, you need only say the word, and I will clear a space in my diary. I hope you will not take my decision as a sign of indifference towards the cause, which I continue to admire deeply. Please accept my warmest thanks once more, and my best wishes for the coming year.

qs.q: Why is the writer sending this message?
o: To decline an invitation to join a committee

qs.q: What is the reason for the refusal?
o: He already has too many commitments

qs.q: What does he offer instead?
o: To review documents or speak at the annual meeting

qs.q: What does he hope?
o: That Helena will visit him soon
That the committee will change its aims

That Helena will not see his decision as indifference

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: why does the writer refuse the invitation, and what does he offer?

C1.title: An Evening Talks Programme
C1.text: The Riverside Museum is delighted to announce a series of evening talks devoted to the history of everyday objects. Each session will be led by a different specialist, who will explore how an apparently ordinary item, such as a key or a clock, has shaped human habits. Rather than presenting dry facts, the speakers have been asked to tell stories and to invite questions throughout. Seating is limited, so early booking is strongly advised, and latecomers cannot be admitted once the doors have closed. Tickets are offered at a reduced rate to students and to anyone over the age of sixty-five. Refreshments will be served in the cafe afterwards, giving guests an opportunity to continue the conversation informally. Those unable to attend in person may follow each talk online, although the recordings will be available for one week only. We look forward to welcoming curious minds of every age and background.

What have the speakers been asked to do?
Why is early booking advised?

C1.title: The Last Customer
C1.text: Henrik had run the small bookshop for thirty years, and on the day it was to close he expected nothing more than a quiet afternoon of packing boxes. Customers drifted in, murmured their regrets, and left without buying anything, which struck him as a fitting end to a long and unprofitable career. Towards closing time, a young woman entered, glanced around the empty shelves, and asked whether he still had a copy of a certain obscure poetry collection. He did, though he had long ago stopped expecting anyone to ask for it. She explained that her late father had written it and that she had searched for years without success. Henrik, who had kept that book on his shelf out of sheer stubbornness, felt his throat tighten. He refused to take her money and wrapped the volume himself, carefully, as if it were fragile. When she had gone, he stood for a while in the silence, then unpacked the boxes and decided that the shop would stay open after all.

What was the young woman looking for?
o: A poetry collection written by her father

qs.q: Why did Henrik refuse to take her money?
o: She did not have enough money

qs.q: How does the story end?
o: He sells the shop to the young woman
He decides to keep the shop open

C1.title: The Friday Market
C1.text: Every Friday the harbour square in the old quarter turns into a market so crowded that one has to move with the crowd rather than through it. Stalls selling spices, secondhand books and hand-woven baskets stand elbow to elbow beneath awnings of faded canvas. The air is thick with the smell of grilled fish, which mingles curiously with that of fresh coffee and warm bread. Vendors call out their prices in a rhythm so practised that it almost resembles singing. Bargaining is not merely tolerated but expected, and a visitor who pays the first price named is regarded with polite amusement. Away from the central aisles, however, the atmosphere changes, and one finds quiet corners where elderly men play cards for hours without exchanging a word. Locals insist that the best bargains are to be had late in the afternoon, when sellers are eager to avoid carrying their goods home. By evening nothing remains except crumpled paper, a few stray cats, and the faint echo of the day's noise.

qs.q: When does the market take place?
How is a visitor who pays the first price named regarded?
What do the elderly men do in the quiet corners?
According to the locals, when are the best bargains found?
o: On the first Friday of the month

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what is the market like, and when are the best bargains?

C1.title: A Town Closes Its Centre
C1.text: A mid-sized town in the south has decided to close its historic centre to private cars, a measure that has divided opinion sharply. The authorities argue that the change will reduce noise and pollution and make the streets safer for pedestrians. Shopkeepers, on the other hand, fear that customers who once parked outside their doors will now choose to shop elsewhere. To address these concerns, the council has promised to provide free shuttle buses and to subsidise deliveries to local businesses. A similar experiment in a neighbouring town was judged a success after a year, although critics point out that the circumstances were not identical. Public meetings held last week were often heated, and several speakers accused the mayor of acting without sufficient consultation. The mayor, for his part, maintains that the decision was taken openly and that the town cannot afford to wait. The restrictions are due to take effect at the start of next spring, once the new bus routes are ready.

qs.q: What has the town decided to do?
o: Close the historic centre to private cars

qs.q: Why are the shopkeepers worried?
How will the council address these concerns?

qs.q: When are the restrictions due to start?
o: At the start of next spring

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: why do people disagree about closing the town centre?

C1.title: In Defence of Boredom
C1.text: We tend to treat boredom as an enemy to be eliminated at the first opportunity, usually with the nearest screen. Yet I would argue that some of our most original thoughts occur precisely when nothing demands our attention. A mind left to wander makes connections that a mind constantly entertained never has the chance to make. Children, in particular, benefit from being left occasionally without a task, since it is in such moments that they invent games and discover their own interests. Parents who rush to fill every free minute with activities may, with the best intentions, be depriving their children of this opportunity. Critics will object that boredom can lead to restlessness, even to mischief, and they are not entirely wrong. But restlessness is often the first stage of creativity, and the discomfort it brings is a small price to pay. We would do well, therefore, to resist the urge to cure it too quickly.

qs.q: How do people usually treat boredom, according to the writer?
o: As an enemy to be removed quickly

qs.q: When do our most original thoughts occur?
o: When we are working under pressure
When we are talking with friends
When we are watching a screen

qs.q: What does the writer say about parents who fill every free minute?
o: They are too strict with their children
They spend too little time with their children
They may be depriving children of the chance to discover their own interests

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude to the critics?
o: They are partly right, but restlessness often leads to creativity
They are experts who should be obeyed

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: why does the writer think boredom can be good for children?

C1.title: Sleep and Memory
C1.text: Scientists believe that sleep plays a central role in turning fleeting experiences into lasting memories. During the day, new information is held temporarily in a region of the brain that has limited capacity. Once we fall asleep, this information is gradually replayed and transferred to areas where it can be stored for the long term. The process is thought to occur mainly during deep sleep, when the brain's electrical activity slows into large, regular waves. Researchers have found that people who learn a list of words in the evening and then sleep recall far more of them than those who stay awake. Sleep also appears to be selective, strengthening the memories that matter most and allowing trivial details to fade. This explains why a night's rest often helps us solve a problem that seemed impossible the evening before. It also suggests that students who sacrifice sleep in order to study may be defeating their own purpose.

qs.q: What role does sleep play, according to scientists?
o: It increases the capacity of the brain
It speeds up the day's learning
It helps turn brief experiences into lasting memories

qs.q: When does the transfer mainly occur?
What did researchers find about people who learned a list of words?
o: Those who stayed awake remembered more
Those who slept afterwards remembered far more
There was no difference between the groups
Those who learned in the morning did better

qs.q: What does this suggest for students?
o: They should study only at dawn
They should avoid learning lists of words
Giving up sleep in order to study may be self-defeating

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: why is sleep important for memory?

C1.title: The Summer of the Flood
C1.text: I was twelve the summer the river burst its banks, and I remember it less as a catastrophe than as an extraordinary holiday. School was cancelled for two weeks, and the lower streets of our town became waterways along which neighbours paddled in whatever they could find. My father, normally a serious and reserved man, spent hours ferrying elderly residents to higher ground in a borrowed rowing boat. I watched him with a mixture of awe and envy, because I had never seen him so openly cheerful. My mother, meanwhile, set up a kitchen in the church hall and fed anyone who turned up, often until well past midnight. It was only later, when the water retreated and left the ruined furniture and sodden carpets behind, that I grasped how much had been lost. Even so, the adults spoke of that fortnight afterwards with a warmth I could not quite account for. Looking back, I believe they were recalling the one time when the whole town had stopped being strangers to one another.

qs.q: How old was the writer in the summer of the flood?
What did the writer's father do?
o: He cooked meals for the neighbours
He took elderly residents to higher ground in a borrowed boat

qs.q: What did the writer's mother do?
o: She set up a kitchen in the church hall

qs.q: Why does the writer think the adults spoke so warmly of that time?

For a short time the town had stopped being a community of strangers

C2.title: The Night Shift
C2.text: Nadia has been on the ward for hours, moving between beds with a lightness of tread that years of practice have made almost instinctive. The corridors, so bustling by day, take on a hushed and faintly nautical quality at night, as though the building were a ship adrift in the dark. She has learned that patients confide in the small hours what they would never admit in daylight, and she listens with an attentiveness that she regards as no less important than any medication. Around three o'clock, when fatigue is at its most treacherous, she makes tea and stands briefly at the window, watching the first delivery vans nose through the empty streets. Colleagues who have never worked nights tend to imagine the job as a lonelier version of the day, but she finds it a different country altogether, with its own customs and its own peculiar tenderness. When the morning staff arrive, full of noise and good intentions, she hands over her notes with a faint reluctance she would find hard to explain. Walking home against the tide of commuters, she feels like a visitor returning from a place that the rest of the world has agreed to forget. She falls asleep to the sound of the city waking, which strikes her as an agreeable irony. By then there is nobody left to share it with.

qs.q: When does Nadia say patients are most willing to confide in her?
What does Nadia do around three o'clock?
o: She falls asleep at her desk
She makes tea and looks out of the window

qs.q: How do colleagues who have never worked nights imagine the job?
o: As a lonelier version of the day

qs.q: How does Nadia feel as she walks home?
o: Like a visitor returning from a place the world prefers to forget
Proud that she has been noticed

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what is special about Nadia's work at night?

C2.title: The Village of My Ancestors
C2.text: I had put off the journey for decades, partly from a vague fear that reality would fail to match the village I had constructed from my grandmother's stories. When at last I stepped off the bus, the place seemed at once smaller and more ordinary than I had imagined, a scatter of low houses clinging to a ridge above a dry riverbed. An old man, noticing my hesitation, asked whom I was looking for, and when I gave my grandmother's maiden name he stared at me as though I had risen from the dead. Within minutes I was being led from house to house, introduced to cousins whose existence had never been mentioned, and pressed to eat food I had no appetite for but could not refuse. It emerged that the family home had long since collapsed, and that only a few stones of the doorway still stood among the weeds. I remember standing before them with a feeling that I can only describe as grief for something I had never possessed. Yet by evening, seated at a crowded table beneath a single bulb, I sensed that the village I had come to find had never been a place at all. It was, rather, the habit of belonging, which these strangers had extended to me without a moment's hesitation. I left the next morning with fewer illusions and, curiously, a far greater sense of home.

o: A fear that reality would not match the imagined village
A dislike of travelling by bus

qs.q: How did the old man react to the maiden name?

He stared as though the writer had risen from the dead

qs.q: What remained of the family home?
o: A few stones of the doorway

qs.q: What did the writer conclude that evening?
o: That the journey had been a mistake

That the village had never been a place but a habit of belonging

C2.title: A Reply About Your Draft
C2.text: Dear Marcus, I am sorry to have taken so long to reply, and I would like to explain, rather than merely excuse, the delay. When your draft arrived, I read it twice and found myself unable to say anything useful, which is an unusual and slightly humbling experience for someone paid to have opinions. The argument is elegant, and the evidence is carefully assembled, yet something about the conclusion seemed to me to promise more than the pages before it had earned. It took me several days to put my finger on the problem, which is that you have answered a question that no reader is yet asking. If you were to open with the puzzle that first drew you to the subject, the conclusion would then arrive as a resolution instead of an assertion. I realise that this is a larger change than you were hoping for, and I will understand if you feel that it distorts your intentions. Nevertheless, I would urge you to consider it before the deadline, because the work deserves to be read as carefully as it was written. Do not hesitate to ring me if you would like to discuss any of this at greater length. In the meantime, please accept my congratulations on a piece of work that is already considerably better than most I see.

o: The draft left the writer unsure what to say at first

o: It answers a question that no reader is yet asking

qs.q: What does the writer suggest?
o: Opening with the puzzle that first drew Marcus to the subject

qs.q: What is the writer's overall opinion of the work?
o: It is already better than most the writer sees

C2.title: A Retreat for Writers
C2.text: Nestled in a remote valley, far from the clamour of towns, the old mill offers a week of uninterrupted solitude to writers who have lost the thread of their work. There is no signal for telephones, no television, and, we regret to say, no apology for either. Each guest is given a small room with a desk beside the window, and meals are delivered quietly to the door at fixed hours so that no thought need be broken by conversation. Evenings, for those who wish it, are spent around a long table where participants may read aloud from their work and receive gentle but honest criticism from the others. A resident editor, whose own books have been translated into many languages, is available each afternoon for private consultations. We make no promises that the week will produce a finished manuscript, since experience has taught us that inspiration cannot be hired by the hour. What we can guarantee is silence, good bread, and the rare permission to take one's own writing seriously. Places are strictly limited to eight, and applicants are asked to send a short sample of their work together with a brief account of what they hope to achieve. Those selected will be informed within a fortnight.

o: A week of television and telephones
A week of uninterrupted solitude for writers

qs.q: How are meals provided?
o: They are served in a busy dining hall

qs.q: What can the organisers guarantee?
o: Silence, good bread and permission to take one's writing seriously

qs.q: How should applicants apply?

C2.title: The Inheritance
C2.text: When the old professor died, he left his entire library to the one student who had never once agreed with him. The other students, many of whom had spent years flattering him in the hope of favour, received nothing but a short note thanking them for their company. Their indignation was loud, and for a while it seemed likely that the will would be contested in court. Yet the chosen heir, a quiet woman named Irena, found herself oddly unmoved by the prospect of ownership and spent the first week simply wandering among the shelves. In almost every volume she discovered marginal comments in her former teacher's cramped handwriting, many of them addressed directly to her, as though he had anticipated her objections decades in advance. Some were mocking, others surprisingly tender, and a few conceded points that he had never admitted aloud. It slowly dawned on her that the argument she had believed they were having in the seminar room had been, for him, an extended conversation he could not bear to end. She did not contest the will, nor did she sell a single book. Instead, she began to answer him in the margins, in a smaller hand, and with considerably better grammar.

o: The students who had flattered him
The one student who had never agreed with him

o: Margin notes, many of them addressed to her

C2.title: The Salt Flats
C2.text: Few landscapes strip away the human scale as thoroughly as the great salt flats, where the horizon dissolves into a pale and shimmering haze and the eye struggles to find anything on which to rest. After rain, a thin sheet of water spreads across the surface, and the sky is reflected so perfectly that visitors report the sensation of walking on the clouds. In the dry season, by contrast, the ground cracks into vast hexagons of white crust that crunch underfoot like frozen snow. The silence is complete and slightly unnerving, interrupted only by the wind, which carries a fine dust that settles in the hair and between the teeth. Photographers are drawn to the place for the optical games it permits, such as pictures in which a person appears to be holding a mountain in the palm of one hand. Local workers, however, regard it as a harvest rather than a spectacle, and they spend long days raking the salt into low heaps to dry in the sun. Their weathered faces and cracked hands bear witness to a labour that tourists rarely stop to consider. At dusk the whole expanse turns the colour of a bruise, then fades to a darkness so deep that the stars seem within reach. It is a place that rewards those who come to look, but it demands a certain humility from those who come to stay.

qs.q: What happens to the salt flats after rain?
o: A thin sheet of water reflects the sky

qs.q: Why are photographers drawn to the place?
o: Because of the colours of the sunrise
Because of the optical games it allows

qs.q: How do the local workers regard the flats?
What does the writer say the place demands of those who stay?

C2.title: An Ancient Boat Is Found
C2.text: Archaeologists working on the northern coast have announced the discovery of a wooden boat that appears to be roughly two thousand years old, a find that has startled even the most seasoned members of the team. Preserved by the oxygen-poor mud in which it had lain, the vessel is almost entirely intact, and the marks of the tools used to shape it can still be seen along its hull. Initial analysis suggests that it was built for trade rather than war, since its wide, shallow frame would have carried heavy cargo but offered little speed. Among the objects recovered from the wreck were pottery jars, a coil of rope, and what appears to be a child's toy, a detail that has moved many who have followed the story. The find has been described in the press as the most significant of its kind in a generation, although the team itself has refrained from such language. The excavation director cautioned against drawing sweeping conclusions, noting that the results of dating tests will not be available for several months. Local officials, however, are already speaking of building a museum on the site, an idea that some residents greet with enthusiasm and others with deep suspicion. Critics fear that the arrival of crowds may damage the very fragile landscape that preserved the boat in the first place. For the moment, the vessel remains beneath a protective cover, and its fate is likely to be debated for some time to come.

qs.q: Why is the boat so well preserved?
o: It was kept inside a dry cave
It was buried in dry sand

qs.q: What was the boat probably built for?
What did the excavation director advise?
o: Not drawing sweeping conclusions before the dating results arrive

qs.q: What do the critics fear?
o: That the museum will be too expensive

That crowds will damage the fragile landscape
That the boat will decay in the open air

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what was found on the coast, and why do people disagree about its future?

C2.title: The Virtue of Slow Reading
C2.text: It has become fashionable to boast of how many books one has read in a year, as though literature were a distance to be covered rather than a country to be explored. I find this habit not merely vulgar but self-defeating, for a book hurried through leaves little more trace than a train glimpsed from a platform. The great novels, in particular, were not written to be consumed at speed, and their richness lies in precisely those passages that the impatient reader skims in search of plot. To linger over a sentence, to return to a paragraph that has puzzled or delighted us, is not a sign of slowness but of attention, which has become the scarcest of modern virtues. Defenders of the numbers game will reply that more reading is always better than less, and in a narrow sense they are right. But a habit that rewards quantity above all else will soon teach us to value quantity above all else, in life as well as in reading. Slowness, after all, is merely the speed at which a good book wishes to be read. I would rather finish ten books that changed me than a hundred that merely passed through. If that makes me a laggard among readers, I accept the title without regret and with a certain private satisfaction.

qs.q: What fashion does the writer criticise?
o: Boasting about how many books one has read

qs.q: To what does the writer compare a book that is hurried through?
o: A train glimpsed from a platform

qs.q: How does the writer describe attention?
o: A habit that can be bought

qs.q: What would the writer prefer?
o: To read a hundred books quickly
To finish ten books that changed him

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: why does the writer prefer to read slowly?

C2.title: How the Tides Are Made
C2.text: The tides, which seem so natural and regular as to require no explanation, are in fact the product of a subtle contest between gravity and motion. The moon pulls most strongly on the side of the Earth nearest to it, drawing the oceans into a bulge that follows it around the planet. Less intuitively, a second bulge forms on the opposite side, because there the moon's pull is weaker than elsewhere and the water is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth rotates beneath these two bulges, any given coast passes through each of them once a day, which is why most places experience two high tides and two low tides within roughly a day. The sun also exerts a gravitational pull, though its greater distance makes its influence less than half that of the moon. When the sun and moon line up, their effects combine to produce unusually large tides, whereas when they stand at right angles to one another they partly cancel and the tides are mild. The shape of the coastline can amplify these movements dramatically, so that in certain narrow bays the water rises and falls by many times the height found in the open sea. Navigators have understood these patterns for centuries, even if the underlying physics remained mysterious until comparatively recent times. It remains remarkable that a force exerted across such an immense distance should lift the sea against the pull of the very planet that holds it.

qs.q: Why does a second bulge form on the side away from the moon?
o: The sun pulls the water there
The moon's pull is weaker there, so the water is left behind
The wind pushes the water there

qs.q: How many high tides do most places experience in about a day?
When are the tides unusually large?
o: When the sun is hidden by clouds
When the sun and moon stand at right angles
When the moon is far away
When the sun and moon line up

qs.q: What can amplify the movement of the water?

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what causes the tides?

C2.title: The Piano in the Hall
C2.text: There was a piano in the hall of the house where I grew up, an upright of no particular distinction that nobody in the family could play. It had been bought by my grandmother in a burst of optimism about the cultural development of her descendants, and it stood for decades as a monument to that unfulfilled hope. We used it mostly as a shelf for keys, letters, and the endless small objects that accumulate in a household, and its lid was seldom raised. Yet I remember, with a clarity that surprises me, the afternoon when a visiting aunt sat down and began to play something slow and unfamiliar. The whole house seemed to stop, and even the dog lifted his head from the rug and regarded her with an expression of grave astonishment. I was perhaps nine, and it had never occurred to me that the thing in the hall was capable of making any sound beyond a hollow thud when I knocked it with my knee. When she finished, she closed the lid, apologised for being out of practice, and returned to the kitchen as though nothing had happened. I have heard a great deal of music since, some of it undoubtedly finer, but none that has ever reordered the furniture of my mind in quite the same way. I suspect that what I heard that afternoon was not so much a melody as a glimpse of what the house had been holding back.

What was the piano mostly used for?
o: A shelf for keys, letters and small objects

qs.q: How did the dog react when the aunt began to play?
o: He ran out of the room

qs.q: What did the aunt do when she finished playing?
o: She closed the lid, apologised and went back to the kitchen
She asked the writer to play
She left the house at once

write.prompt: Write one or two sentences in the language you are learning: what happened on the afternoon the aunt played the piano?
